extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, patent attorneys/agents, and attorneys facing USPTO reciprocal-discipline proceedings (OED, bar counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria the USPTO applies when considering imposition of reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication, including the burden of proof and statutory/regulatory bases for discipline and exceptions. Useful for attorneys/respondents and counsel preparing responses or appeals to USPTO reciprocal-discipline actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford standard (Selling elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: State disbarment creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper unless independent review reveals (1) a want of due process, (2) an infirmity of proof of the misconduct, or (3) that grave injustice would result from the imposition of reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts have generally held that the respondent attorney bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline; this is typically an uphill burden because the norm is to impose discipline substantially similar to that of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d) grounds to avoid identical discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical discipline unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the Director finds, a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) imposition of the same public suspension by the Office would result in grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each enumerated ground is a high-threshold exception to the default of imposing identical discipline; the respondent must produce clear and convincing evidence on one of these specific bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(e) prima facie case rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A final adjudication in another jurisdiction that a practitioner has been guilty of misconduct establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner violated 37 C.F.R. § 10.23, as further identified under 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state disciplinary adjudication therefore typically satisfies the Office's prima facie burden that a practitioner violated USPTO ethics rules, shifting the burden to the respondent to rebut under §11.24(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal discipline cases, it is the respondent attorney's burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling/§11.24(d) elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office and federal precedent treat this as an uphill climb for respondents; bare assertions are insufficient — the respondent must establish a genuine issue of material fact with clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23 — definition of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct. Paragraph (c)(5) explicitly includes 'Suspension or disbarment from practice as an attorney or agent on ethical grounds by any duly constituted authority of a State' as conduct constituting a violation of paragraphs (a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An established suspension in a state on ethical grounds is itself actionable under §10.23(c)(5) without the Office having to relitigate underlying conduct; the Office may find a practitioner unfit to practice based solely on that state suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.20 — disciplinary rules mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary Rules are mandatory in character and state the minimum level of conduct below which no practitioner can fall without being subjected to disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports application of USPTO disciplinary rules as minimum standards for practitioners before the Office; violations trigger mandatory consideration of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority (35 U.S.C. § 32 and § 2(b)(2)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 32 provides that the USPTO has statutory authority to exclude from further practice before the Office any person shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct. Section 2(b)(2)(D) delegates authority to establish regulations that govern conduct of attorneys practicing before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office's disciplinary regulations and powers are grounded in these statutes; they justify reciprocal exclusion/suspension when ethical violations are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pardon on disclosure and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A pardon 'forgives but does not forget'; a pardon does not overturn a judgment of conviction or erase the fact that one was once convicted. For occupational licensing where 'good moral character' is a standard, a pardon does not automatically eliminate consideration of the underlying conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative sources cited include the Nevada Attorney General opinion, the Nevada Board of Pardons Commissioners web statements, and Missouri case law (Guastella). Practitioners should not assume a pardon absolves the duty to disclose arrests/charges or eliminates moral character concerns; relying on an informal statement that it is 'as if it never happened' is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: RPC Rule 4-8.1 — duty to disclose in bar applications and disciplinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant for admission to the bar or a lawyer in connection with a bar admission application or in connection with a disciplinary matter shall not fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension known by the person to have arisen in the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes an ongoing duty to disclose and correct misapprehensions, and continuing failures may constitute misconduct even after admission; concealment on a bar application can form the basis for later discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof standard (how strong infirmity must be)
rubrics_metrics.description: To defeat reciprocal discipline on the basis of infirmity of proof, there must be such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The infirmity must be substantial — not mere disagreement with factual findings; it must be clear and convincing that the proof was inadequate to sustain the state finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process standard (notice and opportunity to be heard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be avoided if 'the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office examines the state proceeding's record for evidence of notice and opportunity; mere displeasure with publicity or use of certain documents is insufficient absent clear deprivation of procedural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of the same public suspension by the Office would result in grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must show that application of identical discipline would be fundamentally unfair under the circumstances (examples considered include reliance on mistaken assurances about pardons or erasure from agency records), but the Office will weigh controlling state and authoritative policies about pardons and moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of conduct (pre-registration misconduct still relevant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical violations that occurred prior to registration before the USPTO may still justify exclusion or suspension; 37 C.F.R. §10.23(c)(5) contemplates discipline based on a practitioner's disbarment in another jurisdiction regardless of when the underlying conduct occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheinbein v. Dudas and related discussion confirm that the Office may exclude based on the state finding of misconduct rather than relitigating when the conduct happened; failing to disclose pre-admission misconduct can constitute ongoing violations (e.g., continued failure to correct a misapprehension).

rubrics_metrics.name: RPC Rule 5.28(e) — minimum default suspension period for undetermined suspensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for good cause shown, no application for reinstatement for a person who is suspended shall be considered until after six months of the date discipline is imposed; where a state imposes suspension for an undetermined amount of time, this rule sets a default minimum suspension period of six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO may apply the state's default minimum suspension period (six months) when imposing reciprocal discipline in cases where the state suspension length is undetermined but governed by rules like RPC 5.28(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office practice on imposing identical discipline and ancillary orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director will impose the identical suspension unless the respondent meets the §11.24(d) exceptions; the Order also specifies ancillary actions such as publication in the Official Gazette, notice to appropriate employees/agencies/states, compliance with duties under 37 C.F.R. §11.58, and eligibility to apply for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. §11.60 after the suspension period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents should expect public notice and administrative requirements accompanying suspensions and should follow the cited procedural rules for reinstatement and compliance while suspended.
